sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Two contracting methods are used for micropile drawings and specifications, chosen by project criticality and complexity, owner experience and contractor availability; both are valid if properly implemented. Method (procedural): all design, materials and methods specified; a variant lets the contractor choose drilling and grouting to reach specified capacities. Performance (end-result): lines, grades, design criteria and performance requirements. Documents performance-based for drilling and grouting are recommended.
sections.body: (p. 9-1) The chapter describes contracting approaches commonly used for contract documents on micropile projects. Two types of contracting methods are used, and agencies may prefer one, the other or a mix, based on the criticality and complexity of the project, the experience of the owner and its consultants, the availability of specialty contractors and the agency's experience with micropiles; both are valid if properly implemented and each has advantages and disadvantages. Method (or Procedural) Approach: all details of design, construction materials and methods are specified in the contract documents; a variant allows the contractor to select the drilling and grouting methods required to achieve specified pile capacities. Performance or End-Result Approach: lines and grades with specific design criteria, methods and performance requirements are provided, and a project-specific review and detailed plan submittal occur with the working drawings. Because specialty contractors often introduce innovative, cost-competitive solutions, contract documents should let them use the latest construction techniques; documents that are performance-based with respect to drilling and grouting methods are recommended, which the performance approach and the variant of the method approach allow.
key_points: Choice of method depends on project criticality and complexity, owner and consultant experience, and specialty contractor availability
Method (procedural) approach: all design details, materials and methods specified
Method variant: contractor selects drilling and grouting methods to achieve specified pile capacities
Performance (end-result) approach: lines, grades, design criteria and performance requirements; detailed plans submitted with working drawings
Recommended: documents performance-based with respect to drilling and grouting, allowed by the performance approach and the method variant
sections.applicability: The two contracting approaches for micropile projects and the recommendation for performance-based drilling and grouting.

sections.title: Contractor Qualification
sections.summary: An experienced, qualified contractor is critical; owner-enforced construction QA raises the chance of success, and owners new to micropiles should engage a qualified third-party QA provider. Documents should define pre-qualification requirements, submittal procedures and enforcement (or experience requirements where formal pre-qualification is not allowed). Minimums: five successful projects in the last five years; a supervising engineer with three years and three projects; three load test reports; superintendents and drill operators with three projects in five years.
sections.body: (pp. 9-1 to 9-2) Micropile construction procedures must be followed closely for a high quality product, and selecting an experienced and qualified contractor is critical to a satisfactory installation; the likelihood of success increases further when the owner develops and enforces comprehensive construction quality assurance procedures. Agencies or owners with no previous micropile experience should seek a qualified third-party quality assurance provider. Contract documents should clearly define (1) the contractor pre-qualification requirements, (2) submittal procedures for this information and (3) how the owner will enforce them; such requirements are commonly used by transportation agencies for other specialty techniques (permanent ground anchors, soil nail walls, drilled shafts, shotcreting). Where formal pre-qualification may not be allowed, agencies should require bidders to demonstrate specific micropile experience. Recommended minimum qualifications: 1. the firm and its proposed employees provide evidence of successful micropile design and installation, with owner references for projects of similar scope, documenting at least five successful projects in the last five years; 2. the firm assigns a supervising engineer with at least three years of experience in micropile design and construction of at least 3 successfully completed projects over the past 5 years; 3. the firm has drilling experience in ground similar to the project and submits at least three successful load test reports from different projects of similar scope; 4. project superintendents and drill operators have micropile installation experience on at least 3 successfully completed projects over the past 5 years.
key_points: An experienced, qualified contractor is critical; owner-enforced construction QA improves success
Owners without micropile experience should engage a qualified third-party QA provider
Contract documents define pre-qualification requirements, submittal procedures and enforcement
Where formal pre-qualification is not allowed, require bidders to demonstrate specific micropile experience
Firm: at least five successful micropile projects in the last five years, with owner references
Supervising engineer: at least three years of micropile experience and 3 completed projects in the past 5 years
At least three successful load test reports from different similar projects; drilling experience in similar ground
Superintendents and drill operators: at least 3 completed micropile projects in the past 5 years
sections.applicability: Pre-qualification and recommended minimum qualifications of micropile contractors.

sections.title: Method Contracting Approach
sections.summary: The method approach provides detailed plans and specifications in the bid documents; it needs agency staff trained in micropiles. The agency is fully responsible for design and performance if components are installed per the documents, and assumes all risk; it is recommended only for agencies with sufficient in-house expertise. In the variant, the contractor develops the required capacity by varying drilling and grouting, hole diameter and length, sharing the capacity risk; the owner and contractor items are listed.
sections.body: (pp. 9-2 to 9-4) The method approach develops a detailed set of plans and specifications for the bidding documents. Its advantage is that complete design details and specifications are developed and reviewed by experienced representatives, and it lets agency engineers examine options during design, but requires engineering staff trained in micropile design and construction, who are then valuable during construction when questions or design modifications arise. The agency is fully responsible for the design and performance of the micropile as long as the contractor installs each component (casing, grout, reinforcement) in strict accordance with the contract documents; it assumes all risks and directs the work if design changes are required by field conditions. A method specification is recommended only for agencies with sufficient in-house expertise that consider micropile design and construction control a conventional or standard method for foundations or slope stabilization. A variant, in which the contractor develops the required pile capacity by varying drilling and grouting methods, hole diameter and pile length from specified minimums, lets contractors use their experience and equipment and shares the major risk (pile capacity for a specified length) with the contractor. The owner typically establishes: scope of work; micropile design loadings and spacing; footing details; corrosion protection; testing procedures and requirements; instrumentation requirements (if any); special design considerations (e.g., scour and liquefaction potential); and performance criteria. The micropile contractor specifies: construction process; micropile type; micropile design; and pile top to footing connection design. This lets qualified specialty contractors provide an economical design meeting the requirements and shares responsibility; it is slightly more restrictive than contractor design/build but still allows some innovation and savings. The owner-controlled design types follow (9.3.1 to 9.3.3).
key_points: Method approach: detailed plans and specifications in the bid documents, needing agency staff trained in micropiles
Agency is fully responsible for design and performance if components are installed per the documents, and assumes all risks
Recommended only for agencies with sufficient in-house micropile expertise
Variant: contractor develops capacity by varying drilling and grouting, hole diameter and length from specified minimums, sharing capacity risk
Owner sets scope, design loads and spacing, footing details, corrosion protection, testing, instrumentation, special considerations, performance criteria
Contractor specifies construction process, micropile type, micropile design and pile top to footing connection
Owner-controlled design types: standard design, alternate micropile design, cost reduction incentive proposal (9.3.1-9.3.3)
sections.applicability: The method contracting approach, its risk allocation, and the variant in which the contractor develops the pile capacity.

sections.title: Standard Design
sections.summary: The owner's engineer provides design loadings, footing design and pile layout, plus geotechnical data, design parameters (maximum pile sizes, axial and lateral loads, displacement and ductility), utility plans, site limitations, submittal requirements, material, testing and instrumentation requirements, acceptance criteria and payment method. Pay per micropile separately for production piles, verification tests and proof tests (add/deduct footage for piles in rock). Contractors bid a preliminary design; the selected contractor's design is approved before construction.
sections.body: (pp. 9-4 to 9-5) The contract documents for the Standard Design Type allow various qualified micropile designs. The owner's engineer provides the micropile design loadings, footing design and pile layout for foundation support, and also: geotechnical reports and data; micropile design parameters (foundation support projects only), including maximum pile sizes, axial and lateral pile loads, displacement requirements and ductility requirements; existing utility plans; site limitations ((1) access, (2) right of way, (3) scour potential, (4) liquefaction potential, (5) noise requirements, (6) vibration requirements, (7) potential hazardous and/or contaminated materials); contractor working drawing/design submittal and review requirements, including time frame and penalties; material specifications; testing requirements; instrumentation requirements (if any); micropile acceptance criteria; and method of measurement and payment. Measurement and payment is recommended on a unit-per-micropile basis separately for (1) furnished and installed production piles, (2) verification testing and (3) proof testing, except that an add/deduct footage price may be included for piles founded in rock. During bidding, micropile contractors prepare a preliminary design and firm cost proposal from the owner's plans and specifications; for subcontracted work, the general contractor includes the best specialty bid and names the recommended micropile subcontractor in its bid. After award, the selected specialty contractor submits working drawings and design calculations for review and approval, and construction begins after acceptance.
key_points: Owner provides design loadings, footing design and pile layout
Owner also provides geotechnical data, design parameters (maximum pile size, axial and lateral loads, displacement and ductility), utility plans
Site limitations listed: access, right of way, scour, liquefaction, noise, vibration, hazardous or contaminated materials
Payment per micropile, separately for production piles, verification tests and proof tests; add/deduct footage for piles in rock
Contractors bid a preliminary design and firm price; the general contractor names the micropile subcontractor
After award, working drawings and calculations are approved before construction
sections.applicability: The standard owner-controlled design type: owner-provided information, payment basis and the bidding sequence.

sections.title: Alternate Micropile Design
sections.summary: The owner provides a base design with a more traditional foundation system, and listed specialty contractors may submit alternate micropile designs on a one-for-one pile replacement basis, with the Standard Design information also required. Alternatively, contractors may submit fewer, higher capacity micropiles while the owner's engineer keeps control of the footing design, with two to three alternative pile footing designs and load criteria shown on the plans.
sections.body: (p. 9-5) For the Alternate Micropile Design method (printed 'Microple'), the owner provides a base design in the contract documents using a more traditional foundation support system, and the documents allow alternate micropile designs to be submitted by the listed specialty contractors on a one-for-one pile replacement of the owner-designed pile system; the information described under the Standard Design Type is also required. Alternatively, the approach can allow micropile contractors to submit designs with fewer, higher capacity micropiles than the conventional pile footing design requires, while the owner's engineer maintains control of the footing design; the contract documents are similar, except that the owner provides two to three alternative pile footing designs on the plans with the associated pile design and load criteria.
key_points: Owner provides a base design with a traditional foundation system
Listed specialty contractors may submit alternate micropile designs as one-for-one pile replacements
Or fewer, higher capacity micropiles, with the owner keeping control of the footing design
Owner then shows two to three alternative pile footing designs with pile design and load criteria
sections.applicability: Owner base design with alternate micropile designs allowed.

sections.title: Cost Reduction Incentive Proposal (Value Engineering)
sections.summary: The Cost Reduction Incentive Proposal is a long-established form of alternate proposal in the United States. Where permitted, the owner should state any additional restrictions, such as right-of-way. Since foundation support elements are usually the first order of work, review and approval must be timely.
sections.body: (pp. 9-5 to 9-6) The Cost Reduction Incentive Proposal is another long-established form of alternate proposal used in the United States. When such proposals are permitted, the owner should specify any additional restrictions that may apply, such as right-of-way restrictions. Foundation support elements are usually the first order of work, so review and approval of the proposal must be performed in a timely manner.
key_points: Cost Reduction Incentive Proposal: long-established US form of alternate proposal
Owner should state additional restrictions, such as right-of-way
Review must be timely because foundation support is usually the first order of work
sections.applicability: Value engineering proposals for micropile work.

sections.title: Performance Specifications
sections.summary: Under 'line and grade' or 'conceptual plans', the agency defines geometry and material specifications, performance requirements including factors of safety, and acceptable construction and design methods. Benefits: design by experienced staff using contractors' proprietary methods, lower agency engineering cost. Drawback: agency engineers need expertise to review designs and modifications. Bids are lump sum or unit price; a special provision sets submittals and schedules. Payment is typically lump sum for design/build proposals, pre-bid or post-bid.
sections.body: (pp. 9-6 to 9-7) This approach is often called 'line and grade' or 'conceptual plans'. The agency (1) prepares drawings defining the geometric requirements and material specifications, (2) defines performance requirements including factors of safety and (3) indicates the range of acceptable construction and design methods. With sound specifications and contractor pre-qualification it offers several benefits: design by trained and experienced staff using contractors' proprietary equipment and methods with routinely used material components, and lower agency engineering costs and manpower, transferring some design cost to construction. The disadvantage is that agency engineers must have adequate expertise to review the design and approve construction modifications, and engage a consultant proficient in micropile technology; the pre-qualification limitations described for the method approach also apply. Bid quantities come from pay limits on the drawings and can be bid lump sum or unit price. The basis for detailed designs submitted after award, and construction control and monitoring requirements, are given in a special provision that identifies required submittals (calculations and shop drawings) and the schedules for submittal and review. In the design/build method (as printed under this heading), the owner's engineer typically provides: scope of work; total structure loads; footing details; corrosion protection; testing procedures and requirements; instrumentation requirements (if any); special design considerations (e.g., scour and liquefaction); and performance criteria. The micropile contractor specifies: construction process; micropile type and quantity; micropile design; revisions to footing details to accommodate the micropile design; and pile top to footing connection design. A design/build proposal is submitted before bid advertisement (pre-bid) or after award (post-bid), and measurement and payment is typically lump sum.
key_points: Performance ('line and grade', 'conceptual plans'): agency sets geometry, material specifications, performance requirements (including factors of safety) and acceptable methods
Benefits: experienced designers can use contractors' proprietary equipment and methods; lower agency engineering cost
Drawback: agency engineers need expertise to review designs and modifications, with a proficient consultant
Bid lump sum or unit price from pay limits on the drawings; a special provision sets submittals and review schedules
Owner provides scope, total structure loads, footing details, corrosion protection, testing, instrumentation, special considerations, performance criteria
Contractor specifies process, micropile type and quantity, design, footing revisions and pile top connection
Design/build proposal pre-bid or post-bid; payment typically lump sum
sections.applicability: The performance ('line and grade') specification approach: agency and contractor roles, benefits and drawbacks.

sections.title: Design/Build Approach
sections.summary: The design/build approach is treated under 9.5.1 General, 9.5.2 Postbid Design and 9.5.3 Prebid Design; no text is printed under this heading.
sections.body: (p. 9-7) No text is printed under this heading; see 9.5.1 General, 9.5.2 Postbid Design (the contents misprint its number as 9.3.2) and 9.5.3 Prebid Design.
key_points: Design/build: general (9.5.1), postbid design (9.5.2), prebid design (9.5.3)
sections.applicability: Pointer to the contractor design/build approach (9.5.1 to 9.5.3).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: In design/build construction the specialty contractor is part of the project team for all foundation and ground-support aspects. The micropile contractor is responsible for the adequacy of the design and construction; the owner is responsible for the accuracy of the information on which the design is based. Two types follow: postbid and prebid design.
sections.body: (p. 9-7) In design/build construction, the specialty contractor becomes an important part of the project team and is involved in all foundation and ground-support aspects of the project. The micropile contractor is responsible for the adequacy of the design and construction, and the owner is responsible for the accuracy of the information on which the design is based. The two recommended types of contractor design/build specifications follow (9.5.2 and 9.5.3).
key_points: Specialty contractor is part of the project team for all foundation and ground-support aspects
Contractor is responsible for adequacy of design and construction
Owner is responsible for the accuracy of the information the design is based on
Two types: postbid design (9.5.2) and prebid design (9.5.3)

sections.title: Postbid Design
sections.summary: Documents allow contractor-designed alternatives; the owner's engineer designs ancillary structures and gives performance criteria and objectives: at least geotechnical data, structure loadings (axial, lateral and moment), utility drawings, design criteria and parameters, site limitations, ancillary structure details, submittal and review requirements and acceptance criteria. Contractors bid a preliminary design and firm price; after award the selected contractor's detailed design is reviewed and approved before construction.
sections.body: (pp. 9-7 to 9-8) The contract documents for the postbid design/build method allow various contractor-designed alternatives. The owner's engineer provides the design and detailing of ancillary structures and the performance criteria and objectives for the micropile system design and installation, including at a minimum: geotechnical reports and data; structure loadings (axial, lateral and moment); existing utility drawings; design criteria and parameters; site limitations (e.g., right of way); design and details of ancillary structures; contractor working drawing/design submittal and review requirements; and micropile acceptance criteria. During bidding, micropile contractors prepare a preliminary design and firm cost proposal; for subcontracted items, general contractors include the best proposals and name the recommended micropile subcontractors in their bids. After award, the selected specialty contractor submits detailed design calculations and working drawings for review and approval, and construction begins after acceptance.
key_points: Contractor-designed alternatives; owner designs ancillary structures and sets performance criteria
Owner provides geotechnical data, structure loads (axial, lateral, moment), utility drawings, design criteria, site limitations, acceptance criteria
Contractors bid a preliminary design and firm price; the general contractor names the micropile subcontractor
After award, detailed calculations and working drawings are approved before construction
sections.applicability: The postbid design/build method: owner-provided information and the bidding and design sequence.

sections.title: Prebid Design
sections.summary: The design is done before bidding: performance criteria and design information are released 60 to 90 days before advertisement; contractors submit final calculations and drawings for approval, and the specialty contractors with approved designs (typically two to three) are listed in the contract documents, often with their proprietary drawings. General contractors take bids from each, on its own design, and name the subcontractor; work can start immediately after award.
sections.body: (pp. 9-8 to 9-9) The prebid design/build documents also allow contractor-designed micropile alternatives; the major difference is the timing of design and bidding. Performance criteria and project design information are usually made available 60 to 90 days before the contract advertisement date. Micropile contractors prepare and submit final design calculations and working drawings for the owner's review and approval; once the designs (typically two to three in total) are approved, a list of specialty contractors with approved designs is included in the contract documents, often with their proprietary working drawings, which illustrate the proposed construction and help general contractors coordinate other tasks. General contractors receive bids from each subcontractor, each bidding only on its own proprietary design, include the best cost proposal and name the recommended micropile subcontractor in their bid. Once the contract is awarded, the general contractor and the specialty micropile contractor can begin work immediately.
key_points: Design precedes bidding: criteria released 60 to 90 days before advertisement
Contractors submit final calculations and drawings for approval; typically two to three designs approved
Approved specialty contractors listed in the contract documents, often with their proprietary drawings
Each subcontractor bids only its own design; work can begin immediately after award
sections.applicability: The prebid design/build method: designs approved before advertisement and the bidding sequence.

sections.title: Contract Plans
sections.summary: For every specification method the plans must give enough information for a bid that meets the owner's objectives; subsurface information, utility plans and micropile design criteria are very important. Inadequate subsurface information and conservative design criteria create expensive contingencies, higher prices and claims. Sample plans and guide specifications: owner-controlled design in Appendix C-1, contractor design/build in Appendix C-2.
sections.body: (p. 9-9) For all of the specification methods, the contract plans must include sufficient information for the contractor to develop a bid proposal that meets the owner's objectives. The quality of the subsurface information, existing utility plan and micropile design criteria is very important for a successful project; inadequate subsurface information and conservative pile design criteria may create expensive contractor contingencies, higher pile prices and increased claim potential. Sample contract plans and guide construction specifications using owner-controlled design methods are provided in Appendix C-1, and using contractor design/build methods in Appendix C-2.
key_points: Contract plans must carry enough information for a bid meeting the owner's objectives
Subsurface information, utility plans and micropile design criteria are very important
Poor subsurface data and conservative criteria cause contingencies, higher prices and claims
Sample plans and guide specifications: Appendix C-1 (owner-controlled design), Appendix C-2 (contractor design/build)
sections.applicability: Information contract plans must give for micropile bids, and the sample plans in Appendix C.
